Combine unprojected depths using a deterministic union operation to form the 3D Gaussian centers [S4].

The claim states that unprojected depths are combined using a deterministic union operation to form 3D Gaussian centers. This is explicitly confirmed in the provided text. Specifically, the 'Source [S4] notes' list includes the bullet point: 'Combine unprojected depths using a deterministic union operation to form the 3D Gaussian centers.' Additionally, the caption for Fig. 2 states: 'The per-view depth maps are unprojected to 3D and combined using a simple deterministic union operation as the 3D Gaussian centers.' Furthermore, the Introduction mentions: 'simply considering the union of the unprojected per-view depth predictions as the global 3D representation.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
Predict opacity, covariance, and color Gaussian parameters jointly with the depth maps in parallel [S4].

The claim states that the model predicts opacity, covariance, and color Gaussian parameters jointly with the depth maps in parallel. This is explicitly confirmed in Source [S4] notes ('Predict opacity, covariance, and color Gaussian parameters jointly with the depth maps in parallel') and in the text passages ('We also learn other Gaussian primitives' parameters jointly with the Gaussian centers...'), ('The opacity, covariance and color Gaussian parameters are predicted jointly with the depth maps'), and ('predict... opacity, covariance... and color... in parallel with the depths').
supported

*   **Output:** A set of $H \times W \times K$ 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by position $\mu_j$, opacity $\alpha_j$, covariance $\Sigma_j$, and color $c_j$ (represented as spherical harmonics) [S4].

The claim states that the output is a set of $H × W × K$ 3D Gaussian primitives defined by position, opacity, covariance, and color (spherical harmonics). Source [S4] explicitly confirms this in Equation (1) and the surrounding text: 'We predict the Gaussian parameters, including position µj, opacity αj, covariance Σj and color cj (represented as spherical harmonics) in a pixel-aligned manner, and thus the total number of 3D Gaussians is H × W × K for K input images with shape H × W.' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported

MVSplat is a feed-forward deep neural network that directly regresses 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) parameters from sparse multi-view images in a single pass, bypassing the per-scene gradient descent optimization loop required by standard 3DGS [S4].

The evidence explicitly states that MVSplat is a 'feed-forward model' (Abstract, Section 1) that predicts '3D Gaussian parameters' (position, opacity, covariance, color) from 'sparse multi-view images' (Abstract, Section 3). It further clarifies that this is done in a 'single forward pass' (Section 1) and is trained 'purely with the photometric loss' (Section 1), which implies it bypasses the per-scene gradient descent optimization loop typically associated with standard 3DGS reconstruction methods that require iterative optimization for each new scene.
supported
Refine the cost volume and predict per-view depth maps using the 2D U-Net [S4].

The claim states that the model refines the cost volume and predicts per-view depth maps using a 2D U-Net [S4]. The provided notes for Source [S4] explicitly list: 'Concatenate Transformer features and cost volumes as input to a 2D U-Net with cross-view attention' and 'Refine the cost volume and predict per-view depth maps using the 2D U-Net.' Additionally, Figure 2 caption in the passages confirms: 'The Transformer features and cost volumes are concatenated together as input to a 2D U-Net (with cross-view attention) for cost volume refinement and predicting per-view depth maps.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
Concatenate Transformer features and cost volumes as input to a 2D U-Net with cross-view attention [S4].

The claim states that Transformer features and cost volumes are concatenated as input to a 2D U-Net with cross-view attention. Source [S4] explicitly confirms this in the notes ('Concatenate Transformer features and cost volumes as input to a 2D U-Net with cross-view attention') and in the caption for Figure 2 ('The Transformer features and cost volumes are concatenated together as input to a 2D U-Net (with cross-view attention)...'). Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
partial
*   **Strengths:** Bypasses per-scene gradient descent; provides useful 3D priors for subsequent 3D optimizations; works on a variety of object types [S5].

The claim contains three distinct points. The evidence supports the points that the model 'provides useful 3D priors for subsequent 3D optimizations' and 'works on a variety of object types' (specifically noting it is trained on all CO3Dv2 categories). However, the evidence does not support the claim that the model 'bypasses per-scene gradient descent.' While the text mentions the model generates reconstructions with a 'single forward pass' and compares it to 'single-scene overfitting methods' (which typically involve gradient descent), it does not explicitly state that the model itself bypasses per-scene gradient descent as a mechanism or feature. In fact, the evaluation regime involves 'finetuning feedforward results,' which implies gradient descent is used in the broader pipeline, even if the initial prediction is feedforward. Therefore, only some facts are supported.
supported
The model uses 10× fewer parameters and infers more than 2× faster than pixelSplat, while providing higher appearance and geometry quality [S4].

The claim states that the model uses 10x fewer parameters, infers more than 2x faster than pixelSplat, and provides higher appearance and geometry quality. The provided evidence explicitly confirms all these points in multiple locations: 1) The notes state 'MVSplat uses 10x fewer parameters and infers more than 2x faster than pixelSplat.' 2) The notes mention that unlike pixelSplat, MVSplat results in 'better geometry'. 3) The abstract and Figure 1 caption explicitly state: 'compared to the latest state-of-the-art method pixelSplat, MVSplat uses 10× fewer parameters and infers more than 2 × faster while providing higher appearance and geometry quality'. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
MVSplat was introduced to combine multi-view feature extraction through transformers and cost volumes, processed by a U-Net, building upon the foundations of PixelSplat [S1].

The claim states that MVSplat builds upon PixelSplat by combining multi-view feature extraction through transformers and cost volumes, processed by a U-Net. The provided text explicitly states: 'MVSplat [58] builds upon PixelSplat by combining multi-view feature extraction through transformers and cost volumes, which are then processed by a U-Net.' This matches the claim exactly.
unsupported

*   **Limitations:** As a feed-forward model, it may not achieve the same level of geometric fidelity as iterative methods that overfit to a specific scene's data, particularly in areas with limited viewpoint coverage [S4].

The claim states that the feed-forward model 'may not achieve the same level of geometric fidelity as iterative methods... particularly in areas with limited viewpoint coverage.' However, the evidence (Source [S4]) explicitly argues the opposite: it claims that MVSplat (the feed-forward model) provides 'higher appearance and geometry quality' compared to the iterative/probabilistic method pixelSplat, and that it avoids the 'noisy geometry artifacts' associated with predicting depth solely from image features. Furthermore, the evidence highlights that MVSplat uses a cost volume to provide 'valuable geometry cues' and achieves state-of-the-art performance, contradicting the claim that it lacks geometric fidelity compared to iterative methods.
supported
*   **Time Complexity:** The method performs inference in a single forward pass, achieving 22 fps on RealEstate10K and ACID benchmarks [S4].

The evidence explicitly states in the Abstract and Section 1 that 'MVSplat achieves state-of-the-art performance with the fastest feed-forward inference speed (22 fps)' on the 'RealEstate10K and ACID benchmarks'. The claim accurately reflects these facts.
supported
*   **Loss Function:** The model is trained end-to-end purely with photometric loss between rendered and ground truth images [S4].

The claim states that the model is trained end-to-end purely with photometric loss between rendered and ground truth images. The provided evidence explicitly confirms this in multiple sections. Specifically, the 'Source [S4] notes' list 'Loss: Photometric loss between rendered and ground truth images.' Furthermore, the text from the paper states, 'Our full model MVSplat is trained end-to-end purely with the photometric loss between rendered and ground truth images.' Additionally, the abstract mentions learning parameters 'while only relying on photometric supervision.' Thus, every fact in the claim is present and supported by the evidence.
supported
*   **Input:** $K$ sparse-view images $I^i \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}$ and their corresponding camera projection matrices $P^i = K_i [R_i | t_i]$ [S4].

The claim states that the input consists of K sparse-view images $I^i$ and corresponding camera projection matrices $P^i$. This is explicitly confirmed in Source [S4], specifically in the 'Notes' section which lists 'Input: K sparse-view images $I^i$... and camera projection matrices $P^i$...', and in the 'Method' section of the text which begins with 'We begin with K sparse-view images I = {I i}... and their corresponding camera projection matrices P = {P i}...'. The notation and variables match exactly.
supported
Unlike typical MVS methods that require ground truth depth supervision, MVSplat is fully differentiable and trained from RGB images alone using only photometric loss [S4].

The claim states that MVSplat is fully differentiable, trained from RGB images alone, and uses only photometric loss, unlike typical MVS methods that require ground truth depth supervision. The evidence in Source [S4] explicitly supports these points: 1) It states 'our model is fully differentiable and does not require ground truth geometry supervision for training' and 'our model is trained from RGB images alone'. 2) It mentions 'Our full model MVSplat is trained end-to-end purely with the photometric loss'. 3) It contrasts this with typical MVS methods, noting 'existing MVS networks... are mostly trained with ground truth depth as supervision' and 'Unlike typical MVS methods with separate depth estimation and point cloud fusion...'. All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
The core intermediate structure is a per-view cost volume that stores cross-view feature similarities for all potential depth candidates, providing geometry cues for depth estimation [S4].

The claim states that the core intermediate structure is a per-view cost volume storing cross-view feature similarities for potential depth candidates to provide geometry cues. Source [S4] explicitly confirms this in the Abstract ('build a cost volume representation via plane sweeping, where the cross-view feature similarities stored in the cost volume can provide valuable geometry cues to the estimation of depth') and in the Introduction ('Specifically, the cost volume stores cross-view feature similarities for all potential depth candidates, where the similarities can provide valuable geometry cues to the localization...'). The notes also confirm the construction of per-view cost volumes using plane sweeping for this purpose.
